MESSAGE:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a name for the delivery van
2. Work out the drop order and timeline meeting all time windows, the break and the 12:00 return  KEY: Only feasible order is B -> A -> C. Leave 08:30, arrive B 08:50, unload to 09:05 (done before 09:30); arrive A 09:30, unload to 09:45 (inside 09:00-10:00); arrive C 10:25, wait until 11:00 (take the 30-min break during this wait); unload 11:00-11:15; back at depot 12:00 exactly (zero slack). A-first fails (B reached 09:40, after opening). Must give order B, A, C with a timeline that respects all constraints.
3. Rewrite the delivery text to be friendlier
4. List three furniture checks before handover
5. Recommend paper vs emailed delivery note
6. Define 'proof of delivery' in a line
7. Draft an evening-before arrival text under 160 characters

ANSWER:
Here's tomorrow sorted.

## 1. Van name ideas

- **Chesterfield**
- **The Dovetail**
- **Woody**
- **Sideboard Sid**
- **The Armoire Express**

## 2. Tomorrow's route: B → A → C, with no time to spare

**B → A → C is the only order that works.**

- **C has to be last,** because it won't accept anything before 11:00.
- **A first doesn't work.** The earliest arrival at A is 09:00. After unloading and driving to B, the van would reach B at 09:40, which is after the shop opens.
- That leaves **B, then A, then C**.

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave the depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at **B**, unload 08:50–09:05 (done well before the 09:30 opening) |
| 09:05 | Drive to A (25 min) |
| 09:30 | Arrive at **A**, unload 09:30–09:45 (within the 09:00–10:00 window) |
| 09:45 | Drive to C (40 min) |
| 10:25 | Arrive near **C**, **30-minute break, 10:25–10:55** |
| 11:00 | Unload at **C**, 11:00–11:15 |
| 11:15 | Drive back to the depot (45 min) |
| **12:00** | **Back at the depot** |

The van gets back at exactly 12:00, with **no spare time at all**. Any delay after B, such as slow unloading at C or traffic on the way back, makes him late. If you can, do one of these:

- Ask office C whether they'd accept a delivery at 10:45 instead. That gives 15 minutes of slack, and the break still fits.
- Agree with whoever set the 12:00 return that a few minutes late is acceptable.
- At the very least, warn the driver that the return is tight, and make sure he keeps C's unloading to 15 minutes.

## 3. Friendlier arrival text

> Hi [Name], it's [Driver] from [Company]. I'm on my way with your furniture and should be with you in about [X] minutes. See you soon!

## 4. Three things to check before handing over furniture

1. **Damage:** check every surface, edge and corner for scratches, dents or chips, ideally with the customer watching.
2. **Completeness:** check that all parts are there, including legs, shelves, keys, handles, glass panels and fittings.
3. **Function:** open and close drawers and doors, check that the piece stands level and doesn't wobble, and test any mechanisms such as extending tables or locks.

Photos of the piece in place before you leave are good protection if a damage claim comes up later.

## 5. Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Email, with a signature on a phone or tablet at the door.** It's harder to lose, the timestamp is automatic, photos can be attached, and the customer gets a copy straight away. Keep a few paper notes in the van for customers who prefer paper or when the phone signal is bad.

## 6. Proof of delivery, in a line

> **Proof of delivery is the record, usually a signature, timestamp and photos, showing the item was handed over to the customer in good condition.**

## 7. Evening-before text

> Hi [Name], your [Company] delivery is due tomorrow [9-10am]. We'll text when on our way. Reply if that's a problem. Thanks!

With the placeholders as written, this is **123 characters**, which leaves about 35 characters for longer names. If your company name is long, check the length of the final text.

**Use a straight apostrophe in "We'll"**, not a curly one, and no emojis. Some phones and texting tools insert a curly apostrophe automatically. A single special character like that switches the whole message to a different encoding with a **70-character** limit, so the text would be split into multiple messages.
